thermodynamics-001.question: At constant temperature and pressure, which quantity and condition correctly determine whether a change in a closed system proceeds spontaneously?
choices: The Gibbs energy change ΔG is negative
The enthalpy change ΔH is negative (exothermic)
The entropy change ΔS of the system alone is positive
thermodynamics-001.explanation: At constant temperature and pressure, a change proceeds spontaneously in the direction that lowers the Gibbs energy of the system, G = H − TS (ΔG < 0), and equilibrium is reached at ΔG = 0. This rewrites the second law, "the entropy of the system plus its surroundings increases", in terms of quantities of the system alone, and the form ΔG = ΔH − TΔS takes both enthalpy and entropy into account. Even an exothermic reaction with negative ΔH does not proceed at high temperature if its entropy falls sharply. Even if the ΔS of the system is positive, a strongly endothermic change does not proceed at low temperature. The entropy of the system alone decides the matter only for an isolated system, which exchanges neither heat nor work with its surroundings.

thermodynamics-002.question: Which statement is correct for a reaction with ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0 (for example, the thermal decomposition of a carbonate)? Assume ΔH and ΔS do not depend on temperature.
choices: It is not spontaneous at any temperature
It proceeds more readily the lower the temperature, and does not proceed above a certain temperature
It becomes spontaneous above a certain temperature
thermodynamics-002.explanation: With ΔG = ΔH − TΔS and both ΔH and ΔS positive, the ΔH term wins at low temperature and ΔG > 0, but as the temperature rises the −TΔS term grows, and ΔG < 0 for T > ΔH/ΔS. Decomposition reactions that release a gas and raise the entropy, and the melting of solids and evaporation of liquids, are of this type; the melting and boiling points are exactly the temperatures at which ΔG = 0. Proceeding more readily at low temperature and not at high temperature is the case ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0, which includes the oxidation of most metals. Not proceeding at any temperature is the case ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0.

thermodynamics-003.question: For the decomposition of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), take the standard reaction enthalpy as ΔH° = +178 kJ/mol and the standard reaction entropy as ΔS° = +161 J/(mol·K), both independent of temperature. Which value is closest to the temperature at which decomposition starts to proceed spontaneously in the standard state with a CO₂ partial pressure of 1 bar (the temperature at which ΔG° = 0)?
choices: About 833 K
About 1106 K
About 1379 K
thermodynamics-003.explanation: Setting ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = 0 gives T = ΔH°/ΔS° = 178×10³ J/mol ÷ 161 J/(mol·K) ≈ 1106 K, which is about 833℃ on the Celsius scale. Above this temperature ΔG° < 0, and decomposition proceeds even with a CO₂ partial pressure of 1 bar. About 833 K takes the Celsius value, obtained by subtracting 273 from the absolute temperature, and attaches the unit K to it. About 1379 K is the value obtained by adding 273 instead. Dividing ΔH° in kJ by ΔS° in J gives about 1.1 K, so it is also important to make the units consistent. In the actual calcining of limestone, lowering the CO₂ partial pressure lets decomposition proceed at lower temperatures.

thermodynamics-004.question: In an Ellingham diagram, what is the main reason why the ΔG° line for the oxidation of most metals, 2M(s) + O₂(g) → 2MO(s), slopes upward, with ΔG° becoming larger (closer to 0) at higher temperature?
choices: Gaseous O₂ is consumed to form a solid oxide, so the entropy change ΔS° is negative
As temperature rises, the heat ΔH° released by oxidation grows
As temperature rises, faster diffusion in the metal increases the oxidation rate
thermodynamics-004.explanation: An Ellingham diagram plots ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° for oxide formation per mol of O₂ against temperature, and if ΔH° and ΔS° are roughly constant, the slope of the line is −ΔS°. In metal oxidation, high-entropy gaseous O₂ is taken into a solid, so ΔS° is negative, around −0.2 kJ/(mol·K), and the slope is positive (upward). In other words, oxides become less stable at higher temperature. ΔH° depends little on temperature and only sets the height of the line. Diffusion and oxidation rates belong to kinetics and have nothing to do with the slope of the Ellingham diagram, which represents the equilibrium ΔG°. At the temperatures where a metal or oxide melts or boils, ΔS° changes and the line bends.

thermodynamics-005.question: Which statement correctly describes the line for the carbon reaction 2C(s) + O₂(g) → 2CO(g) in an Ellingham diagram?
choices: Like C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔS° is nearly 0, so the line is horizontal
Like metal oxidation, ΔS° is negative, so the line slopes upward and carbon becomes a weaker reducing agent at higher temperature
The gas increases from 1 mol to 2 mol, so ΔS° is positive, the line slopes downward, and carbon becomes a stronger reducing agent at higher temperature
thermodynamics-005.explanation: In 2C + O₂ → 2CO, the gas increases from 1 mol of O₂ to 2 mol of CO, so ΔS° is positive (about +0.18 kJ/(mol·K)) and the ΔG° line slopes downward. As a result, at higher temperatures the CO line lies below the lines of many metal oxides, and carbon becomes able to reduce those oxides. This is why iron ore can be reduced with coke in a blast furnace. In C + O₂ → CO₂ the number of gas molecules does not change and ΔS° is nearly 0, so it is this reaction whose line is nearly horizontal. An upward slope is the case for metal oxidation, in which gaseous O₂ is taken into a solid.

thermodynamics-006.question: In an Ellingham diagram, the formation reactions of all oxides are drawn with ΔG° normalized per mol of O₂. What is the main advantage of doing so?
choices: All the ΔG° values become positive and lie above the temperature axis, so the scale is easier to read
The vertical distance between 2 lines is directly equal to the ΔG° of the reaction in which one metal reduces the other's oxide
The ΔS° that sets the slope becomes equal for all oxides, so the lines can be compared as parallel lines
thermodynamics-006.explanation: With normalization per mol of O₂, taking the difference between, for example, 4/3 Al + O₂ → 2/3 Al₂O₃ and 2Fe + O₂ → 2FeO cancels the O₂, and the ΔG° of 2FeO + 4/3 Al → 2Fe + 2/3 Al₂O₃ can be read directly as the vertical distance between the 2 lines. The metal of the lower line can reduce the oxide of the upper line at that temperature. The ΔG° of oxide formation is almost always negative, and the normalization does not change its sign. The slopes are set by the ΔS° of each reaction, so they do not become equal even when normalized per mol of O₂. In metal oxidation, 1 mol of gaseous O₂ is consumed in every case, which only makes the slopes similar.

thermodynamics-007.question: At 1000℃, take ΔG° for 4/3 Al + O₂ → 2/3 Al₂O₃ as −850 kJ/mol and ΔG° for 4/3 Cr + O₂ → 2/3 Cr₂O₃ as −530 kJ/mol (both per mol of O₂). Which combination of the ΔG° of 2/3 Cr₂O₃ + 4/3 Al → 2/3 Al₂O₃ + 4/3 Cr and the direction in which the reaction proceeds is correct? Assume all substances are pure.
choices: −320 kJ/mol; it proceeds in the direction of aluminum reducing Cr₂O₃
+320 kJ/mol; it proceeds in reverse, in the direction of chromium reducing Al₂O₃
−1380 kJ/mol; it proceeds in the direction of aluminum reducing Cr₂O₃
thermodynamics-007.explanation: The required reaction is the Al₂O₃ formation equation minus the Cr₂O₃ formation equation, and the O₂ cancels. ΔG° = (−850) − (−530) = −320 kJ/mol is negative, so the reaction proceeds in the direction of aluminum reducing Cr₂O₃ to give metallic chromium. This corresponds to the Al₂O₃ line lying below the Cr₂O₃ line in the Ellingham diagram, and it is the principle of making metallic chromium by the aluminothermic process. +320 kJ/mol reverses the order of subtraction and gets the sign wrong; because Al₂O₃ is the more stable oxide, chromium does not reduce Al₂O₃. −1380 kJ/mol is the value obtained by adding the 2 ΔG° values.

thermodynamics-008.question: At 1000 K, ΔG° for 2Ni(s) + O₂(g) → 2NiO(s) is −298 kJ/mol. Which value is closest to the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure at which Ni and NiO coexist? Treat Ni and NiO as pure solids (activity 1), and take the standard pressure as 1 bar, the gas constant as 8.314 J/(mol·K), and ln 10 = 2.303.
choices: About 1×10⁻³⁶ bar
About 2×10⁻⁸ bar
About 3×10⁻¹⁶ bar
thermodynamics-008.explanation: At equilibrium ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln(1/pO₂) = 0, so ΔG° = RT ln pO₂. Then log pO₂ = ΔG°/(2.303RT) = −298000/(2.303 × 8.314 × 1000) ≈ −15.6, and pO₂ ≈ 3×10⁻¹⁶ bar. If the oxygen partial pressure of the atmosphere is higher than this, Ni is oxidized; if it is lower, NiO is reduced. About 1×10⁻³⁶ bar mistakes ΔG°/RT ≈ −35.8 for a common logarithm instead of a natural logarithm. About 2×10⁻⁸ bar takes ΔG° per mol of NiO (−149 kJ/mol), drops the exponent 1/2 on pO₂, and sets it equal to RT ln pO₂.

thermodynamics-009.question: At 1000 K, take ΔG° for 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g) as −385 kJ/mol and ΔG° for 2Ni(s) + O₂(g) → 2NiO(s) as −298 kJ/mol. When nickel is annealed in an H₂–H₂O gas mixture, which value is closest to the partial pressure ratio pH₂O/pH₂ at which Ni and NiO are in equilibrium (Ni is not oxidized if the ratio is smaller than this)? Take the gas constant as 8.314 J/(mol·K), and treat Ni and NiO as pure solids.
choices: About 5.3×10⁻³
About 190
About 3.5×10⁴
thermodynamics-009.explanation: Taking the difference of the 2 equations gives 2Ni + 2H₂O → 2NiO + 2H₂, with ΔG° = (−298) − (−385) = +87 kJ/mol. At equilibrium ΔG° = −RT ln K with K = (pH₂/pH₂O)², so (pH₂O/pH₂)² = exp(87000/(8.314 × 1000)) = exp(10.46) ≈ 3.5×10⁴, and pH₂O/pH₂ ≈ 190. As long as the water vapor pressure is less than about 190 times that of hydrogen, Ni is not oxidized. About 3.5×10⁴ forgets that H₂ and H₂O each appear as 2 mol in the equation and omits the square root, and about 5.3×10⁻³ inverts the ratio to pH₂/pH₂O.

thermodynamics-010.question: Which statement about the activity of a component in a solution (a liquid or a solid solution) is correct?
choices: Activity is always equal to the molar concentration (mol/L), and the activity coefficient does not depend on the kind of solution
The activity coefficient is greater than 1 (positive deviation from Raoult's law) when unlike atoms attract each other more strongly than like atoms
Taking the pure solid or liquid as the reference (activity 1), the activity of a component in an ideal solution is equal to its mole fraction
thermodynamics-010.explanation: Activity a is a "thermodynamic effective concentration" defined so that the chemical potential of a component in a solution can be written μ = μ° + RT ln a. With the pure substance as the reference state, the activity of a pure solid or liquid is 1, and in an ideal solution a = x (the mole fraction) by Raoult's law. For real solutions one writes a = γx, and the activity coefficient γ expresses the deviation from ideality. When unlike atoms attract each other more weakly than like atoms, the component escapes from the solution more easily, giving γ > 1 (positive deviation) and a tendency toward phase separation. When unlike atoms attract strongly, γ < 1, indicating a tendency toward ordering or compound formation. Treating activity as the molar concentration is only an approximation for dilute aqueous solutions.

thermodynamics-011.question: At a certain temperature, let p₀ be the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure at which pure Cr and Cr₂O₃ coexist. At the same temperature, about how many times p₀ is the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure at which an alloy with a Cr activity of 0.10 coexists with pure Cr₂O₃? Take the reaction as 4/3 Cr + O₂ → 2/3 Cr₂O₃.
choices: About 10 times
About 22 times
About 100 times
thermodynamics-011.explanation: At equilibrium ΔG° = −RT ln K, with K = a(Cr₂O₃) to the power 2/3 ÷ (a(Cr) to the power 4/3 × pO₂). At the same temperature ΔG° and K are the same, so with a(Cr₂O₃) = 1, a(Cr) to the power 4/3 × pO₂ is constant. Therefore pO₂ = p₀ × 0.10 to the power −4/3 ≈ 21.5 p₀, about 22 times. Cr in the alloy becomes harder to oxidize to the extent that its activity is lowered, and a higher oxygen partial pressure is needed. About 10 times takes the coefficient 4/3 of Cr as 1, and about 100 times takes it as 2. In this way, the activities of alloying elements and the oxygen partial pressure let you judge which element is selectively oxidized at the surface of a stainless steel.

thermodynamics-012.question: Which statement about the Gibbs energy of mixing of an ideal solution (ideal solid solution), ΔG_mix = RT[x ln x + (1 − x) ln(1 − x)], is correct? x is the mole fraction of one component.
choices: It is negative at all compositions and its slope tends to minus infinity as x → 0, so a tiny amount of solute dissolves in any substance
It arises from the enthalpy of mixing, so it is independent of temperature and turns positive at some compositions, causing separation
It reaches its largest positive value at x = 0.5, and compositions close to a pure substance mix less readily
thermodynamics-012.explanation: In an ideal solution the enthalpy of mixing is 0, and ΔG_mix = −TΔS_mix arises only from the entropy of mixing. For 0 < x < 1, ln x is negative, so ΔG_mix is negative at all compositions and takes its minimum value RT ln 0.5 at x = 0.5 (about −5.76 kJ/mol at 1000 K). As x → 0, the slope d(ΔG_mix)/dx = RT ln[x/(1 − x)] tends to minus infinity, so dissolving even a tiny amount of solute always lowers the free energy. This is the thermodynamic reason why it is difficult to make a perfectly pure substance. ΔG_mix is proportional to T and has nothing to do with enthalpy. What is largest at x = 0.5 is the entropy of mixing; ΔG_mix is at its minimum there.

thermodynamics-013.question: In the regular solution model, the enthalpy of mixing is taken as ΔH_mix = Ωx(1 − x) (Ω is an interaction parameter independent of temperature), and the entropy of mixing is the same as for an ideal solution. For Ω = +20 kJ/mol, which value is closest to the critical temperature Tc = Ω/(2R) at which the region where the solid solution separates into 2 phases (the miscibility gap) disappears? Take the gas constant as 8.314 J/(mol·K).
choices: About 601 K
About 2406 K
About 1203 K
thermodynamics-013.explanation: Tc = Ω/(2R) = 20000/(2 × 8.314) ≈ 1203 K. This formula is obtained as the temperature at which the second derivative of ΔG_mix, −2Ω + RT/[x(1 − x)], becomes 0 at the symmetric composition x = 0.5. Below Tc, the middle of the ΔG_mix curve becomes convex upward and 2 minima appear, so separating into 2 phases of different composition lowers the free energy. Above Tc, the contribution of the entropy of mixing wins, and a single-phase solid solution forms at all compositions. About 601 K uses 4R in the denominator, and about 2406 K uses R. If Ω is negative (unlike atoms attract), no miscibility gap forms, and there is a tendency toward ordering or compound formation.

thermodynamics-014.question: At constant temperature and pressure, which is the correct condition for an α phase and a β phase of a binary system to coexist in equilibrium?
choices: Each component has the same chemical potential in the α and β phases
The Gibbs energy per mole of the α phase is equal to that of the β phase
The α and β phases have equal compositions, with no difference in concentration between them
thermodynamics-014.explanation: At equilibrium, moving a small amount of any component from the α phase to the β phase must not change G, so μA(α) = μA(β) and μB(α) = μB(β) hold for components A and B respectively. When the molar Gibbs energy is plotted against composition, this corresponds to drawing a tangent common to the 2 curves, and the 2 points of tangency give the compositions of the 2 phases in equilibrium. The values at the ends of the tangent (x = 0 and x = 1) are the chemical potentials of the respective components. The molar Gibbs energies of the 2 phases are generally not equal, and the compositions at the 2 ends of the common tangent differ. Equal molar G is the equilibrium condition only when the 2 phases have the same composition, as in the melting of a pure substance.

thermodynamics-015.question: A solid solution with a miscibility gap was quenched from the single-phase state at high temperature and held at a temperature inside the gap. Which statement about spinodal decomposition is correct?
choices: It occurs at compositions where the free energy curve is convex downward (d²G/dx² > 0), and an energy barrier to form a critical nucleus must be overcome
It occurs at compositions where d²G/dx² < 0; there is no nucleation barrier, and composition fluctuations grow by uphill diffusion
It is a diffusionless shear transformation that changes only the crystal structure, keeping the parent phase's composition
thermodynamics-015.explanation: Even inside the miscibility gap, within the spinodal, where the free energy curve is convex upward (d²G/dx² < 0), even a slight composition fluctuation lowers the free energy, so the fluctuations are amplified as they are. There is no nucleation barrier, and atoms diffuse from the low-concentration side to the high-concentration side, against the concentration gradient (uphill diffusion). The result is a fine structure, uniform throughout, in which the composition varies periodically with a certain wavelength. At compositions where d²G/dx² > 0 (between the spinodal and the solubility line), small fluctuations raise the free energy, so separation occurs by the nucleation-and-growth mechanism that forms critical nuclei. A diffusionless shear-type transformation is a martensitic transformation. The 475℃ embrittlement of Fe-Cr ferrite is an example of spinodal decomposition.

thermodynamics-016.question: A metal has a melting point of 727 °C at 1 atm. Take the molar volume change on melting as ΔV = +0.50 cm³/mol and the heat of fusion as ΔH = 10.0 kJ/mol, and treat the Clausius–Clapeyron slope dT/dP = TΔV/ΔH as independent of pressure. Which is closest to the change in melting point when the pressure is raised by 1.0 GPa?
choices: A rise of about 50 K
A rise of about 36 K
A fall of about 50 K
thermodynamics-016.explanation: T in the equation is the absolute temperature, so T = 727 + 273 = 1000 K. dT/dP = 1000 × 0.50×10⁻⁶ m³/mol ÷ 10.0×10³ J/mol = 5.0×10⁻⁸ K/Pa, so raising the pressure by 1.0×10⁹ Pa raises the melting point by about 50 K. About 36 K uses the Celsius value 727 directly as T. A fall of about 50 K has the wrong sign: for a substance whose volume increases on melting (ΔV > 0), pressure favors the denser solid and raises the melting point. Conversely, for substances whose volume decreases on melting, such as ice, bismuth, gallium and silicon, pressure lowers the melting point. The large rise in the melting point of iron under the high pressures inside the Earth can also be understood from this relation.

thermodynamics-017.question: The amount (concentration) of hydrogen dissolved in a metal often follows Sieverts' law with respect to the pressure pH₂ of the hydrogen gas in equilibrium with it. At the same temperature, by roughly what factor does the dissolved amount change when pH₂ is quadrupled?
choices: About 4 times
About 2 times
About 16 times
thermodynamics-017.explanation: When hydrogen dissolves in a metal, it enters not as H₂ molecules but split into atoms. For the equilibrium ½H₂(g) → H (in metal), the equilibrium constant is [H]/pH₂^(1/2), so the dissolved amount is proportional to the square root of the pressure (Sieverts' law). Quadrupling pH₂ multiplies the dissolved amount by √4 = 2. About 4 times applies Henry's law, for gas dissolving as molecules in proportion to pressure, and about 16 times assumes proportionality to the square. Diatomic gases such as N₂ and O₂ that dissolve in metals as atoms follow the same form. This relation is why vacuum degassing removes hydrogen and nitrogen from molten steel, and why lowering the hydrogen partial pressure of the atmosphere helps prevent hydrogen cracking in welds.

thermodynamics-018.question: At room temperature and 1 atm the Gibbs energy change for diamond turning into graphite is negative (about −2.9 kJ/mol), yet diamond does not turn into graphite however many years pass. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Even with a negative ΔG, a reaction whose ΔG is smaller in magnitude than about RT is thermodynamically ruled out from proceeding, so diamond cannot change at all
At room temperature and 1 atm diamond is the more stable phase, and the sign of ΔG has been read the wrong way round
Thermodynamics sets the direction of change but not its rate; the activation energy for rearranging bonds is large, so it is extremely slow at room temperature
thermodynamics-018.explanation: ΔG < 0 shows only the direction in which a change can occur; it says nothing about how fast it proceeds. Turning diamond into graphite requires breaking strong covalent bonds and rearranging how the carbon atoms are bonded, and the activation energy for this is so large that the rate at room temperature is effectively zero. A state that is not the most stable thermodynamically but persists because change is slow is called metastable. Many materials exploit metastable states, such as martensite in quenched steel, rapidly cooled glasses and precipitates partway through aging. Any negative ΔG, however small, permits the change, so the claim that a small value prevents it is wrong. Graphite is the stable form at room temperature and 1 atm; diamond becomes stable on the high-pressure side.

thermodynamics-019.question: For many metals, the entropy of fusion at the melting point Tm, ΔSm = ΔHm/Tm, takes nearly the same value (Richards's rule). Which correctly pairs the content of this rule with what can be inferred from it?
choices: ΔSm is about the gas constant R (about 8.3 J/(mol·K)), so the heat of fusion grows roughly in proportion to the melting point
ΔSm is about 88 J/(mol·K), so the heat of fusion is nearly the same for every metal regardless of melting point
ΔSm is nearly zero, so melting involves no disordering of the atomic arrangement and occurs through the enthalpy change alone
thermodynamics-019.explanation: For many metals the entropy increase from disordering the atomic arrangement on melting is nearly the same, and ΔSm is about the gas constant R (about 8.3 J/(mol·K)). Since ΔHm = TmΔSm, the heat of fusion is roughly proportional to the melting point; for copper, with a melting point of about 1358 K, ΔHm ≈ 8.3 × 1358 ≈ 11 kJ/mol, close to the measured value of about 13 kJ/mol. The relation is often used to estimate the driving force for solidification, ΔG ≈ ΔHmΔT/Tm ≈ ΔSmΔT. About 88 J/(mol·K) is the value of Trouton's rule for the entropy of vaporization of liquids. Melting is a loss of order from solid to liquid, so ΔSm is positive, not zero. For covalently bonded substances such as silicon, ΔSm is larger than this.

thermodynamics-020.question: In a dilute solution of a very small amount of solute B in solvent A, which pair of relations often holds? Take pure substances as the reference for both activities.
choices: Being dilute, both solvent and solute behave ideally, with activity coefficients of 1 and activities equal to their mole fractions for both components alike (Raoult's law)
The solvent's activity nearly equals its mole fraction (Raoult), and the solute's is proportional to its mole fraction with a coefficient not necessarily 1 (Henry)
The solute's activity is always 1 regardless of its mole fraction, and the solvent's activity is proportional to the square of its mole fraction
thermodynamics-020.explanation: In a dilute solution, solvent atoms are surrounded almost entirely by other solvent atoms, so the solvent is close to its pure state and its activity nearly equals its mole fraction (Raoult's law, γA → 1). Solute atoms, by contrast, are surrounded entirely by solvent atoms, an environment quite different from the pure substance. If the solute is scarce enough, however, solute atoms hardly ever meet, and their environment is the same regardless of concentration, so the activity is proportional to the mole fraction and the activity coefficient γB° is a constant not necessarily equal to 1 (Henry's law). When handling the activities of solutes such as carbon and oxygen in steel, a reference of a 1 mass% solution based on this relation is often used. Treating the solute as ideal too is limited to ideal solutions of similar A and B.

thermodynamics-021.question: Which statement about the values listed in thermodynamic tables for pure iron (α-iron) at 298 K and 1 bar is correct?
choices: For an element, both the standard enthalpy of formation and the standard entropy are defined as zero by convention
The standard enthalpy of formation is positive, and the standard entropy is defined as zero as a reference
The standard enthalpy of formation is zero by convention, but the standard entropy is positive, not zero
thermodynamics-021.explanation: The standard enthalpy of formation is a relative quantity, measured from the element in its most stable form at that temperature as the zero reference, so for α-iron at 298 K it is zero. Entropy, by contrast, is an absolute quantity that the third law sets to zero for a perfect crystal at 0 K, and it is found by integrating the heat capacity from 0 K to 298 K. The standard entropy of iron is therefore not zero but a positive value of about 27 J/(mol·K). Making both zero wrongly applies the enthalpy convention to entropy. A positive enthalpy of formation also contradicts the convention for elements. When calculating ΔS° of a reaction, the values for elements must be included, not dropped.

thermodynamics-022.question: For an ideal solid solution of five elements mixed in equal mole fractions (0.2 each), a high-entropy alloy, which is closest to the entropy of mixing per mole, ΔS_mix = −R Σ xᵢ ln xᵢ? Take the gas constant as 8.314 J/(mol·K).
choices: About 5.8 J/(mol·K)
About 13.4 J/(mol·K)
About 66.9 J/(mol·K)
thermodynamics-022.explanation: With xᵢ = 0.2 for each element, ΔS_mix = −R × 5 × 0.2 × ln 0.2 = R ln 5 ≈ 8.314 × 1.609 ≈ 13.4 J/(mol·K). For n components in equal mole fractions, ΔS_mix = R ln n, which grows with the number of components. About 5.8 J/(mol·K) is the equimolar binary value R ln 2 and does not reflect the number of components. About 66.9 J/(mol·K) adds five terms without multiplying by xᵢ, giving 5R ln 5, which is not a per-mole value. At high temperature the −TΔS_mix term weighs heavily, so even with many elements the alloy tends to form a simple solid solution rather than separate intermetallic compounds; this is the idea behind high-entropy alloys. Actual phase stability, however, also depends on the enthalpy of mixing.

thermodynamics-023.question: For a binary A–B solution, the molar Gibbs energy G_m is plotted against the mole fraction of B, x_B. When a tangent is drawn to the curve at some composition, what do the values of the tangent at x_B = 0 and x_B = 1 represent?
choices: The value at x_B = 0 is the chemical potential of A, μ_A, at that composition, and the value at x_B = 1 is that of B, μ_B
The value at x_B = 0 is the chemical potential of B, μ_B, at that composition, and the value at x_B = 1 is that of A, μ_A
Whatever composition the tangent is drawn at, they equal the molar Gibbs energies of pure A and pure B
thermodynamics-023.explanation: G_m = x_A μ_A + x_B μ_B, and with the Gibbs–Duhem equation the slope of the tangent is dG_m/dx_B = μ_B − μ_A. Extending this tangent to x_B = 0 gives μ_A and to x_B = 1 gives μ_B, so the heights of its two ends give the chemical potentials of the components at that composition. Changing the point of tangency changes the slope and the end values, so they equal the Gibbs energies of the pure substances only when the tangent is drawn at a pure composition. Swapping which end corresponds to A and B is wrong. A common tangent to the curves of two phases makes μ_A and μ_B each equal in both phases, which gives the two-phase equilibrium compositions.

thermodynamics-024.question: At 298 K and 1 bar, the Gibbs energy change for graphite → diamond is +2.9 kJ/mol. The molar volumes are 5.31 cm³/mol for graphite and 3.42 cm³/mol for diamond, both taken as independent of pressure. Using (∂ΔG/∂P)_T = ΔV, which is closest to the pressure at which graphite and diamond are in equilibrium at 298 K? Treat 1 bar as negligible compared with the result.
choices: About 1.5 MPa
About 0.85 GPa
About 1.5 GPa
thermodynamics-024.explanation: ΔV = 3.42 − 5.31 = −1.89 cm³/mol = −1.89×10⁻⁶ m³/mol, so at pressure P, ΔG = 2900 + ΔV·P, which falls as pressure rises. ΔG = 0 at P = 2900/(1.89×10⁻⁶) ≈ 1.5×10⁹ Pa, about 1.5 GPa. Denser diamond becomes stable at high pressure. About 1.5 MPa results from converting cm³ as 10⁻³ m³, an error of three orders of magnitude, and about 0.85 GPa uses the molar volume of diamond itself in place of ΔV. This estimate is rough because it ignores compressibility. Actual synthesis uses even higher pressures together with temperatures above 1000 °C or metal catalysts so that the change proceeds at a useful rate.

thermodynamics-025.question: On an Ellingham diagram, the ΔG° line for 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO becomes abruptly steeper (rises more steeply) above the boiling point of Mg (about 1090 °C). What is the reason?
choices: Above the boiling point MgO melts to a liquid, raising the entropy of the product, so ΔG° suddenly increases
Above the boiling point solid MgO forms from gaseous Mg and O₂, so more gas is consumed and ΔS° becomes even more negative
Above the boiling point Mg becomes a gas and the heat of reaction ΔH° approaches zero, so ΔG° rapidly approaches zero
thermodynamics-025.explanation: The slope of the line is −ΔS°. Below the boiling point, solid MgO forms from solid or liquid Mg and 1 mol of gaseous O₂, and ΔS° is negative mainly because O₂ disappears. Above the boiling point the reacting Mg is also a gas, so 3 mol of gas (2Mg + O₂) disappear into a solid, ΔS° becomes even more negative, and the line abruptly steepens. MgO melts at about 2800 °C, far above this range, so the statement that MgO melts is wrong; melting of a product would in any case raise its entropy and make the slope shallower. ΔH° changes by the heat of vaporization of Mg but does not approach zero. Because of this bend, the MgO line can cross the lines of other oxides at high temperature.
